title: Area III review: Preflight Preparation
intro: These questions mix the three Tasks of Area III: pilot qualifications, airworthiness requirements and weather information. Many join two of them in one real instructing situation, such as a learner's go or no-go morning, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: Your private pilot learner wakes with a mild head cold. She took no medicine and says she feels fine, and her medical is current. Her written day VFR ceiling minimum is 2,500 ft, the RMH sample baseline, and the TAF for her local flight shows BKN028 all morning. How do you coach the decision?
options: Go: the medical is current, she took no medicine, and 2,800 ft is above her 2,500 ft minimum

The AIM's safest rule is not to fly with any illness, and she should ask an AME if that seems too strict for this cold. Even then, the RMH has her add at least 500 ft to the ceiling for illness, which makes it 3,000 ft or more, above the forecast 2,800 ft, so it is a no-go today
Add 1/2 mile to her visibility minimum for the illness and go, since the ceiling is above her minimum
Go: the RMH adjustments apply only to night flights
questions.why: Even a minor illness can seriously degrade piloting tasks. The safest rule is not to fly while suffering from any illness, and if that seems too stringent the pilot should contact an Aviation Medical Examiner [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. A current medical does not settle fitness for today. For personal minimums, a pilot facing illness adds at least 500 ft to the ceiling: 2,500 + 500 = 3,000 ft, which is above the forecast BKN028 [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. The 1/2 mile visibility adjustment is for an unfamiliar airplane or avionics, not for illness, and the adjustments are not limited to night [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

questions.q: On a clear, calm fall morning your student finds the club airplane's annual, ELT and transponder all current and every paper in place. The wings carry a thin layer of frost about as rough as sandpaper. He says, "The records prove it's airworthy, so a little frost is just a preflight detail." How do you correct him?
options: He is right: the records settle airworthiness, and frost that thin does not change lift
Only a mechanic may decide whether frost makes the airplane unairworthy, so call maintenance first
Frost matters only if he later flies into icing conditions, so he may depart and let the sun melt it in the climb

Airworthy also means in condition for safe operation, which the PIC decides; frost no rougher than coarse sandpaper can cut lift by 30 percent and raise drag up to 40 percent, so all of it comes off before flight
questions.why: Airworthy means the airplane conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation, and the PIC is responsible for deciding whether it is in condition for safe flight [[24:38|AFH 2-1]] [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]]. The records answer only the first half. Frost, snow or ice no thicker or rougher than coarse sandpaper on the leading edge or upper wing can reduce lift by 30 percent and increase drag up to 40 percent [[28:249|AWH 20-7]], so remove all of it during the preflight. A heated hangar works if the airplane is dry before it goes back outside, or the water refreezes [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4]]. Departing with it ignores the lift loss at takeoff, and the safe-flight call belongs to the PIC, not to maintenance.

questions.q: During runup, an instrument-rated renter you are checking out sees the vacuum gauge at zero and the attitude indicator tumbling. His destination is forecast to be in IMC at his arrival. He says he has a meeting he cannot miss and can fly partial panel if he must. How does the AIH's analysis of its Mooney accident frame this?
options: Low risk: he is instrument rated, partial panel is a trained skill, and the meeting is not a safety factor
Medium risk, acceptable if he files IFR, because ATC can help him in IMC
Only an aircraft hazard; the weather and the meeting are separate questions

The hazards stack across PAVE: the failed pump (aircraft), the IMC (environment), the meeting (external pressure) and his belief he can fly with critical instruments out (pilot). Catastrophic severity with occasional or probable likelihood is high risk and needs mitigation, such as staying out of the IMC
questions.why: In the AIH case the pilot knew the vacuum pump had failed and IMC lay ahead. The equipment was an aircraft hazard, the IMC an environment hazard, the wish to reach the destination likely an external pressure, and the assumption that he could control the airplane with critical instruments inoperative a pilot hazard. Catastrophic consequences with occasional or probable likelihood put it in the high-risk area, and his most effective mitigation may have been to divert and land while still in VMC [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. Before flying with any inoperative item, AC 91-67A asks for a risk analysis that covers the failure itself, adverse weather, workload and other human factors [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. Calling it low risk or an aircraft-only problem ignores how the hazards combine.

questions.q: On October 27, 2026 a renter plans an October 30 flight with flight following, so he will use the transponder. His flight review was October 6, 2024. The airplane's records show an annual on October 21, 2025, a transponder test and inspection on September 29, 2024, and an ELT inspection on December 3, 2025. Which item stops the plan as written?
options: The flight review, because 24 months from October 6, 2024 ran out on October 6, 2026
The annual, because 12 calendar months from October 21, 2025 ended on October 21, 2026
The transponder: its 24 calendar months ran out at the end of September 2026, so it may not be used until it is tested and inspected again
Nothing; every item is good through at least October 31, 2026
questions.why: The flight review counts from the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month of the flight, which is October 2024 for an October 2026 flight, so it is good through October 31, 2026 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. The annual must be within the preceding 12 calendar months, which run from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year, so October 21, 2025 covers through October 31, 2026 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. The ELT inspection is good through December 31, 2026 [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. The transponder must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months before it is used [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]: September 29, 2024 ran out on September 30, 2026. The first two answers make the counting-to-the-day error.

questions.q: Your student's destination is a small field with an AWOS but no TAF. She plans to use the TAF for a larger airport 25 NM away as her destination forecast, since it is the closest one. What do you teach?
options: That is sound: a TAF covers the area within 25 NM of its airport

A TAF covers only the area within 5 SM of the center of its runway complex, so treat it as one clue and use the GFA, which shows forecast clouds, flight category, precipitation and wind for the whole area
Use the destination AWOS instead, since an AWOS issues a new forecast every 20 minutes
Use the TAF as is: a TAF is written for the airport and everything within about 50 NM of it
questions.why: A TAF is a forecast for the area within 5 SM of the center of the airport's runway complex [[28:407|AWH 27-6]], so it does not describe a field 25 NM away. The GFA is meant to give a complete picture of the weather that may affect flight, including forecast clouds, flight category, precipitation, icing, turbulence and wind, and it shows the TAFs and ceiling and visibility forecasts too [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]]. An AWOS generates a METAR every 20 minutes [[28:288|AWH 24-4]]: an observation, not a forecast.

questions.q: Your student is ready to depart when a SPECI comes out: in 10 minutes the wind went from 200 degrees at 14 kt to 300 degrees at 18 kt gusting 28, and the temperature and dewpoint both dropped sharply. A front was forecast to pass this afternoon. What do you teach?
options: The 100 degree shift in under 15 minutes, with 10 kt or more throughout, met the SPECI wind shift criterion; with gusty wind and a fast drop in temperature and dewpoint, the cold front is likely passing now
A SPECI corrects an observer's error, so wait for the next routine METAR before deciding
This is a warm front, because warm fronts bring the sharpest wind shifts
A wind shift alone cannot trigger a SPECI, so the visibility must have dropped as well
questions.why: A SPECI is issued when the wind direction changes by 45 degrees or more in less than 15 minutes with 10 kt or more throughout [[28:290|AWH 24-6]]; 200 to 300 degrees is a 100 degree shift. During cold front passage the winds become variable and gusty and the temperature and dewpoint drop rapidly, and the front leaves gusty, turbulent wind behind it [[1:304|PHAK 12-20]]. Shifting wind is most pronounced with cold fronts, not warm fronts [[1:305|PHAK 12-21]]. So check the gusts against your student's wind limits before going.

questions.q: A Convective SIGMET covers your student's planned route for an area of embedded thunderstorms with tops to FL350. He reads it twice and says, "It says nothing about turbulence or icing, so those are not forecast." How do you answer?
options: Any Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear, and the AIM treats storms with tops of 35,000 ft or more as extremely hazardous
He is right: a Convective SIGMET covers only the hazards printed in its text
Turbulence and icing come only in AIRMETs Tango and Zulu, so check whether those are posted
Embedded storms matter only to IFR traffic, so a VFR flight can continue below the clouds
questions.why: Convective SIGMETs are issued for embedded thunderstorms, among other things, and any Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]. The AIM says to regard as extremely hazardous any thunderstorm with tops of 35,000 ft or higher, and not to fly under a thunderstorm even if you can see through to the other side [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]]. AIRMETs cover moderate turbulence and moderate icing, a lower level than these storms bring [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]].

questions.q: Late on a summer afternoon your student will fly west to an airport reporting 6 SM in haze and land toward the low sun. He says 6 SM is plenty. What should he expect?
options: Haze visibility is the same in every direction, so 6 SM will look like 6 SM on final
Haze forms in unstable air and clears quickly, so it will be gone by his arrival

In haze, air-to-ground slant visibility is poor and visibility varies greatly with whether he faces into or away from the sun, so the runway may be much harder to see on a westbound final than the report suggests
Haze limits only air-to-air visibility, so the runway will be easy to find but traffic will be hard to see
questions.why: Haze occurs in stable air and is usually only a few thousand feet thick. Above the layer, air-to-air visibility is unrestricted, but at or below it the slant range (air-to-ground) visibility is poor, and visibility in haze varies greatly depending on whether the pilot faces into or away from the sun [[28:229|AWH 18-9]]. Haze also clears more slowly than fog, because it must be dispersed by moving air [[28:229|AWH 18-9]]. The last answer has the two kinds of visibility backward.

questions.q: You and your student are holding short on a hot afternoon. A thunderstorm is building near the field, with streaks of rain falling from its base that do not reach the ground and a ring of blowing dust beneath it. Your student says, "It's not even raining on the runway; let's go." What do you teach?
options: Virga and a ring of blowing dust can be the only visible clues to a microburst, which can bring downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 kt; do not take off in the face of the storm, wait it out, and expect more than one
Virga evaporates before it reaches the ground, so it is harmless; depart and expect light chop
A microburst always shows a heavy rain shaft at the surface, so with a dry runway there is none
Depart now, before the storm reaches the field, and climb out beneath it to get on top
questions.why: Microburst activity may show as an intense rain shaft, but virga at the cloud base or a ring of blowing dust is sometimes the only visible clue. A typical microburst lasts about 5 to 15 minutes and can produce downdrafts of up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 kt [[28:263|AWH 22-8]]. More than one can occur in the same system, so stay alert for others [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. The AIM says not to land or take off in the face of an approaching thunderstorm [[34:119|AIM 7-1-27]] and not to fly under one [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]], which rules out the last answer.

questions.q: Your private pilot learner moved across the state seven weeks ago and has not told the FAA his new permanent mailing address. He wants to fly a local flight today. What do you tell him?
options: He may fly: his certificate has no expiration date, so an address change does not matter
He may fly solo but may not carry passengers until he updates the address
He has 90 days, the same as landing currency, so he still has time
After 30 days from the move he may not exercise his certificate privileges until he has notified the FAA Airman Certification Branch in writing of the new permanent mailing address
questions.why: A holder of a pilot certificate who changes permanent mailing address may not, after 30 days from that date, exercise the certificate's privileges unless the FAA Airman Certification Branch has been notified in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]. Seven weeks is 49 days, past the limit. The certificate itself has no expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)]], but the right to use it can still lapse, which is the point to teach. The rule has no solo exception and no 90-day period.

questions.q: Your learner's written day VFR minimums match the RMH sample: a 2,500 ft ceiling, 4 miles visibility and 10 kt of surface wind. Saturday she will fly a club airplane with an avionics suite she has never used, and two friends are counting on the trip. She feels well and is current. Using the RMH adjustments, what are her minimums for this flight?
options: Ceiling 2,500 ft, visibility at least 4 1/2 miles, wind no more than 5 kt
Ceiling at least 3,000 ft, visibility 4 miles, wind 10 kt
Ceiling at least 3,000 ft, visibility at least 5 miles, wind no more than 5 kt
No change: she is current, and the adjustments apply only to pilot factors
questions.why: The RMH adjusts the baseline by risk factor. An unfamiliar airplane or unfamiliar avionics adds at least 1/2 mile to visibility, and external pressures such as passengers subtract at least 5 kt from wind limits. The 500 ft ceiling increase is for pilot factors such as illness, fatigue or lack of currency, which she does not have [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. So 4 + 1/2 = 4 1/2 miles and 10 - 5 = 5 kt, with the ceiling still 2,500 ft [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Currency does not cover new avionics: the FAA recommends a comprehensive checkout in each make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

questions.q: A private pilot (ASEL) who has flown only tricycle-gear airplanes wants to rent a 180-hp, fixed-gear, fixed-pitch tailwheel airplane and take his brother along. Last week he made 3 full-stop landings in a Cessna 172. What must happen before he carries his brother as PIC?
options: Nothing: his ASEL rating covers every single-engine land airplane and he is passenger current
A high-performance endorsement, because the engine is more than 160 hp
Logged tailwheel training and a tailwheel endorsement, then 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane within the preceding 90 days
Only the tailwheel endorsement; the 172 landings keep him passenger current, since the category and class are the same
questions.why: To act as PIC of a tailwheel airplane, a pilot needs logged flight training in one, including normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings and go-arounds, and an endorsement from an authorized instructor [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(i)]]. To carry persons in a tailwheel airplane, the 3 takeoffs and 3 landings in the preceding 90 days must be to a full stop in an airplane with a tailwheel, so the 172 landings do not count [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)]]. A high-performance airplane has an engine of more than 200 horsepower, so 180 hp needs no such endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].

questions.q: Laying out the papers on the wing, your student reads the Certificate of Aircraft Registration: issued March 12, 2023. Today is October 27, 2026. What do you teach?
options: It expired March 31, 2026, three years after the last day of the month of issue, so the airplane needs an effective registration before it flies
It is still effective: it expires seven years after the last day of the month of issue, on March 31, 2030, and the holder may renew during the six months before that date
Registration certificates have no expiration date, like the standard airworthiness certificate
It is good until March 2033, ten years after issue
questions.why: A Certificate of Aircraft Registration expires seven years after the last day of the month in which it was issued, and the holder may renew it during the six months before the expiration date [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40]]. Seven years after March 31, 2023 is March 31, 2030, so it is effective today. The aircraft must carry an effective U.S. registration certificate [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]], and the registration must be in the aircraft at all times [[1:236|PHAK 9-6]]. The no-expiration idea fits the airworthiness certificate, which is a separate requirement and has no printed expiry [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]]. Neither three years nor ten years appears in the rule.

questions.q: Your sport pilot learner owns a standard-category airplane that is within the sport pilot aircraft limits, so she may fly it on her sport pilot certificate. She asks to replace a burned-out landing light bulb herself and sign it off. What does Part 43 say?
options: She may do the work and approve it, since replacing landing light bulbs is on the Appendix A list
She may do the work, but you must sign the return to service

She may not: a sport pilot may do preventive maintenance only on an aircraft she owns or operates that has a light-sport special airworthiness certificate, and approving it in a standard-category airplane takes at least a private pilot certificate
She may do it because she owns the airplane; the kind of airworthiness certificate does not matter
questions.why: Replacing bulbs of position and landing lights is preventive maintenance [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(17)]]. Pilot certificate holders other than sport pilots may do it on an aircraft they own or operate, but a sport pilot may do preventive maintenance only on an aircraft she owns or operates that has a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. After pilot preventive maintenance, at least a private pilot certificate is needed to approve the return to service, except that a sport pilot may approve a light-sport category aircraft she owns or operates [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]] [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(h)]]. Flying the airplane under 61.316 does not change its airworthiness certificate.

questions.q: Your night-current private pilot learner is invited to fly a friend's amateur-built experimental airplane on an evening sightseeing flight that will run well into the night, with the friend aboard. The airplane's operating limitations give no authorization for night flight. What do you teach?
options: Experimental aircraft have no limits beyond the pilot's own currency, so his night currency settles it
Experimental aircraft may fly at night but may never carry passengers
Night flight is allowed once the airplane has the 91.205(c) night equipment, since 91.205 applies to every powered aircraft

Unless the FAA specifically authorizes it, an experimental airplane is flown VFR by day only, so the flight cannot run into the night; he must also tell his friend the aircraft is experimental and tell ATC when using its services
questions.why: Each person operating an aircraft with an experimental certificate must advise each person carried of its experimental nature, operate under VFR, day only, unless specifically authorized by the Administrator, and notify ATC of its experimental nature when using air traffic services [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319(d)]]. 91.205 applies to powered civil aircraft with standard airworthiness certificates [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]], so night equipment alone does not authorize night flight in a special-certificate aircraft. Currency is a pilot requirement and cannot lift an aircraft limitation.

questions.q: An A&P rerigged the ailerons on your learner's own airplane and approved it for return to service. Your learner, a private pilot, wants his wife aboard on the first flight to save time. What does 91.407 require?
options: Nothing more: the mechanic's return to service also clears passengers
The operational check must be flown by the mechanic who did the work
The operational check must be flown by a flight instructor

Since the work may have appreciably changed the flight characteristics, no one but crewmembers may be carried until a pilot rated for the aircraft with at least a private certificate flies an operational check and logs it in the aircraft records, unless ground tests or inspection show conclusively nothing changed
questions.why: No one may operate an aircraft after maintenance until it is approved for return to service and the entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. When the work may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics, no person other than crewmembers may be carried until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies it, makes an operational check and logs the flight in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]]. The flight is not needed if ground tests or inspection show conclusively that nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]]. Your learner may fly the check himself; the rule does not require a CFI or the mechanic.

questions.q: Your student pilot calls from a stop on her solo cross-country. Flight Service said "VFR flight not recommended" for the return leg, but the METARs show 4 SM and a 3,500 ft ceiling. The limitations you wrote in her logbook require at least 5 SM for solo. She asks whether the briefer's statement means she legally may not fly. What do you teach?
options: Yes: "VFR flight not recommended" is a prohibition for student pilots

No: the statement is advisory and the decision is hers, but she is bound by 61.89 (3 SM by day and visual reference to the surface) and by the limitations you wrote in her logbook, so with 4 SM against your 5 SM limit she may not go
No: 4 SM is above the 3 SM student pilot minimum, so she may depart
She may go if she stays below the clouds and keeps visual reference to the surface
questions.why: "VFR flight not recommended" is advisory in nature; the final decision on whether the flight can be made safely rests with the pilot [[28:26|AWH 3-3]]. A student pilot may not act as PIC with flight or surface visibility below 3 SM by day, when the flight cannot be made with visual reference to the surface, or contrary to any limitation an authorized instructor placed in her logbook [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)]]. Your 5 SM limit is part of the law for her, so 4 SM keeps her on the ground even though it meets the regulatory 3 SM.

questions.q: An instrument-rated renter last logged six approaches, holding and course tracking in May 2026 and has not flown IFR since. On October 28 he wants to fly to an airport forecast OVC004, close to the approach minimums. He asks you to confirm he is legal. What is the best answer?
options: He is IFR current, since May falls within the 6 calendar months before October, but currency events five months old may not give him the proficiency for low ceilings; treat the rule as a minimum and suggest practice or instruction first
He is not IFR current, because more than six months have passed since May
He is current and therefore proficient, because the regulation sets the skill level needed
He needs an instrument proficiency check, because more than 90 days have passed
questions.why: IFR currency needs the tasks within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]; for an October flight that is April through September 2026, which includes May. An instrument proficiency check is needed only after more than six calendar months without meeting 61.57(c) [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)]]. The RMH uses this very case: currency events five months old may leave the pilot without the proficiency to fly low ceilings safely [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. Recent experience rules are minimums to be adjusted for the pilot and the environment [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]].

questions.q: Your student departs at 1300Z with an ETA of 1530Z. The destination TAF shows good VFR, then FM151600 OVC008 3SM BR. He says the change comes after he lands, so it does not matter. What do you teach?
options: He is right: a TAF change after the ETA plays no part in the plan

AC 91-92 has him review the destination forecast from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, 1430Z to 1630Z here; the FM group replaces all earlier conditions at 1600Z with an IFR ceiling, so it belongs in his plan, with an alternate if needed
FM means the change could come at any time in the TAF, so he should treat the whole forecast as IFR
An FM group is less than 50 percent likely, so it can be left out of planning
questions.why: Review the destination forecast, including significant changes expected within 1 hour before and after the ETA, and select an alternate airport if needed [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.6]]. With a 1530Z ETA that window is 1430Z to 1630Z, and a small delay puts him at the field after 1600Z. An FM group starts a complete new set of forecast conditions at its time [[28:417|AWH 27-16]], and an 800 ft ceiling is IFR [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]. FM is not a probability group; TEMPO is the one for conditions more than 50 percent likely in brief spells [[28:417|AWH 27-16]].

questions.q: Your pre-solo learner has canceled three lessons in a row, each time saying the weather looked "iffy," though every briefing showed favorable conditions. All three lessons were landing practice before her first solo. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Praise the caution, since a learner can never cancel too often for weather
Require her to fly the next lesson regardless, so the habit does not grow
Consider that the canceling may come from worry about the lesson content, such as landings or the coming solo, and try explaining the maneuver in more detail or offering extra encouragement
Lower her personal minimums so that fewer days look marginal to her
questions.why: If a learner consistently decides not to fly even though weather briefings show favorable conditions, it may be apprehension about the lesson content; stalls, landings or an impending solo may cause concern. Explaining a specific maneuver in greater detail or offering more encouragement may ease that stress [[25:28|AIH 1-24]]. Forcing the flight ignores the cause, and personal minimums should never be adjusted to make a specific flight happen [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

questions.q: On a first lesson, a 17-year-old tells you he wants to fly for an airline someday and plans to get his medical certificate "once solo is close." What does the AIM advise you to tell him?
options: Wait until solo is close, so the medical does not run out before he needs it

See an Aviation Medical Examiner as soon as possible, to avoid wasted training expense if he cannot meet the standards, and since he plans a commercial career, apply for the highest class of medical he might need
Get a third-class medical now and a first-class only after he holds a commercial certificate
Train under BasicMed until he is 18, then apply for an FAA medical
questions.why: Student pilots should visit an Aviation Medical Examiner as soon as possible in their training, to avoid unnecessary training expense should they not meet the standards, and a student who plans to enter commercial aviation should apply for the highest class of medical certificate the career might need [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. BasicMed is not a starting point: it requires having held an FAA medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006 [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(B)]].

questions.q: On preflight your student finds the right fuel gauge reading empty with that tank full. The airplane is a non-turbine single with no MEL. He says he will stick the tanks before each flight, have you agree it is not a hazard, and placard the gauge "INOP" under 91.213(d). What do you teach?
options: That works: a pilot's hazard determination and a placard satisfy 91.213(d)
That works once a mechanic deactivates and placards the gauge
It cannot be deferred: 91.205(b) requires a fuel gauge for each tank on day VFR, so the 91.213(d)(2) test fails; get it repaired, or fly it under a special flight permit
It may be deferred for day VFR but not for night, since only the night list requires fuel gauges
questions.why: Day VFR requires a fuel gauge indicating the quantity of fuel in each tank [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. Under 91.213(d)(2), an item required by 91.205 for the kind of operation may not be inoperative, so the hazard determination and placard steps are never reached [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. An aircraft with inoperable equipment may still be operated under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]. The fuel gauge is on the day list, so the last answer has it backward, and a mechanic's deactivation does not fix a required item.
